items.name: TU Munich (TUM)
items.description: One of Germany's leading technical universities in engineering, computer science, and natural sciences.
history: TUM was founded in 1868 by King Ludwig II of Bavaria as the Polytechnische Schule München. Its name changed several times over the decades, becoming the Technische Hochschule München in 1901 and finally the Technische Universität München in 1970.

Today the university is a member of TU9, the alliance of Germany's nine leading technical universities, and holds "University of Excellence" status from the federal government. It maintains a comprehensive research infrastructure across engineering, computer science, natural sciences, and medicine.

TUM's campuses span three main areas: the historic main campus in central Munich, the Garching campus focused on natural sciences and engineering, and the Weihenstephan campus focused on agriculture and life sciences. The university has produced numerous Nobel laureates throughout its history.
highlights: Strong research infrastructure in engineering, computer science, and natural sciences
Member of the TU9 alliance and holder of "University of Excellence" status
Large, specialized research campuses in Garching and Weihenstephan
Home to some of Germany's most sought-after engineering programs
pros: A globally top-ranked name in engineering and technology
Close proximity and strong internship ties to major industry players like BMW and Siemens
Strong research infrastructure and funding opportunities
cons: Very high admission competition, especially in programs like computer science
Munich is one of Germany's most expensive cities
Crowded lecture halls in popular courses

quickFacts.language: Mostly English at master's level, partly German at bachelor's

items.name: LMU Munich
items.description: One of Germany's oldest and most established universities, strong in medicine, law, and social sciences.
history: LMU was founded in 1472 in Ingolstadt by Duke Ludwig IX of Bavaria. It moved to Landshut in 1800 and then to its current home in Munich in 1826 — the "Ludwig-Maximilians" in its name honors the two rulers associated with that journey.

One of Europe's oldest universities, LMU has been home to numerous Nobel laureates throughout its history, including Wilhelm Röntgen, Max Planck, and Werner Heisenberg. Members of the White Rose (Weiße Rose), the student resistance group that opposed the Nazi regime during World War II, were also LMU students.
Today, with a strong faculty in medicine, law, natural sciences, and social sciences, LMU teaches on a historic campus stretching along Ludwigstraße in the heart of Munich.
highlights: One of Germany's oldest and most prestigious universities
Strong research tradition in medicine, law, and natural sciences
Home to numerous Nobel laureates throughout its history
A city-center campus in the heart of Munich
pros: An extremely broad program range from the humanities to medicine
Strong international reputation for research
A vibrant student life in Munich
cons: High grade requirements (Numerus Clausus) and competition for popular subjects
Munich's high cost of living
Large student body can mean less individual attention in big introductory lectures

quickFacts.language: Mostly German, English options at master's level

items.name: Humboldt University of Berlin
items.description: A research university with international recognition in the humanities and social sciences.
history: Founded in 1810 by the linguist and statesman Wilhelm von Humboldt, Humboldt University is Berlin's oldest university. Its founding gave rise to the "Humboldtian model," which champions the unity of teaching and research under the principle of academic freedom — a model that became the foundation of the modern research university worldwide.

Throughout its history, figures such as Albert Einstein, Max Planck, Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, and Karl Marx have been associated with the university, and numerous Nobel laureates have taught or studied there.

Located on Unter den Linden boulevard in the very center of Berlin, the university suffered heavy damage during World War II and stood within East Berlin during the country's division; its rebuilt historic main building remains the heart of the university today.
highlights: The institution where the modern research university concept was born
International recognition in the humanities and social sciences
Historical ties to figures like Einstein and Planck
A historic campus in central Berlin, on Unter den Linden
pros: A central Berlin location close to cultural and career opportunities
A strong academic reputation in the humanities and social sciences
A historic, internationally recognized name
cons: Berlin's fast-rising rents put pressure on student budgets
High admission competition for popular subjects
A large, bureaucratic university structure can feel impersonal at first

quickFacts.language: Mostly German, some English-taught master's programs

items.name: RWTH Aachen
items.description: One of Europe's leading technical universities in engineering and computer science.
history: Founded in 1870 as the Polytechnicum, RWTH Aachen is today a member of the TU9 alliance and one of Germany's largest technical universities. Its location near the Belgian and Dutch borders has given the university a strong, international network of industry partnerships.

Known for its close ties to industry in automotive and mechanical engineering, RWTH Aachen also takes an innovative approach to student services: its iconic SuperC building, opened in 2009, serves as a central hub for student affairs and advising.

With a high share of international students and a wide range of English-taught master's programs, the university is one of the most popular destinations in Germany for international students seeking an engineering education.
highlights: Strong industry ties in automotive and mechanical engineering
Member of the TU9 alliance of technical universities
An innovative approach to student services via the iconic SuperC building
High share of international students, with English-taught master's programs

items.name: University of Mannheim
items.description: Home to one of Germany's top business and economics programs.
history: Founded in 1907 as the Handelshochschule Mannheim (Mannheim Commercial College), the institution was established through the efforts of then-mayor Otto Beck and economist Eberhard Gothein. Absorbed into the University of Heidelberg under the National Socialist regime in 1933, it reopened after the war in 1946 and gained full university status in 1967.

The university is housed in the historic Mannheim Palace (Schloss Mannheim), Europe's second-largest Baroque palace after Versailles — a distinctive setting that visually sets it apart from other German business schools.
Today, Mannheim consistently ranks among the top German universities for business and economics, with a strong international exchange network and a research-driven academic culture.
highlights: One of Germany's top business and economics faculties
Housed in the historic Mannheim Palace, Europe's second-largest Baroque palace
A strong international exchange program network
A research-driven academic culture with international recognition

items.name: Munich University of Applied Sciences
items.description: A Fachhochschule with strong industry ties in applied engineering and business programs.
history: Formed in 1971 through the merger of seven technical and vocational colleges, Hochschule München is today Bavaria's second-largest university of applied sciences (Fachhochschule).

Offering an education tightly linked to industry in engineering, design, and business, the university introduces students to the working world before graduation through applied project work and mandatory internship periods.
The campus's landmark "Roter Würfel" (Red Cube) building houses the design faculty and is part of a community of around 18,000 students.

Strong industry ties in engineering, design, and business
An applied, internship-driven education model
A community of around 18,000 students

A more direct, career-focused path than a theory-heavy Universität

items.name: Frankfurt University of Applied Sciences
items.description: Applied programs in business and information technology in the financial hub of Frankfurt.
history: Founded on August 1, 1971, Frankfurt UAS is today one of Germany's largest universities of applied sciences, home to more than 15,000 students.

Located in Germany's financial capital, the university leverages its position to build close partnerships with the banking, finance, and IT sectors, offering industry-facing programs in business, information technology, engineering, and social work.
Through applied research projects and mandatory industry internships, the university aims to give its students a strong, direct path into the job market after graduation.

Applied programs in business, IT, and engineering

items.name: DHBW (Baden-Württemberg Cooperative State University)
items.city: Stuttgart, Mannheim, Karlsruhe, and other campuses
items.description: The pioneer of the dual studium model in Germany, alternating theory and practice in three-month cycles.
history: DHBW's roots trace back to the Berufsakademie Baden-Württemberg, founded in 1974. Conceived as an entirely new type of educational institution at the time, it grew quickly to include locations across the state.

In 2009, the Baden-Württemberg state parliament granted this 35-year-old, successful model full higher-education status, transforming the Berufsakademie into the Duale Hochschule Baden-Württemberg (DHBW). By that point, enrollment had surpassed 23,000 students, working with more than 8,000 partner companies.

Today, spread across numerous campuses throughout Baden-Württemberg and working with thousands of partner companies, DHBW offers students a model that alternates theory and practice in three-month cycles, and is considered the pioneer of Germany's dual studium system.

A network of thousands of partner companies
Numerous campus locations across Baden-Württemberg

items.name: IU International University of Applied Sciences
items.description: One of Germany's largest private higher education institutions for dual studium and distance learning.
history: Founded in 1998 in Bad Honnef and Bonn as the Internationale Fachhochschule with just 23 students in its first year, the institution entered a period of rapid growth. It merged with the Adam-Ries-Fachhochschule in 2013, was renamed IUBH Internationale Hochschule in 2017, and took its current name, IU International University of Applied Sciences, in 2021.
Through this rapid expansion, IU has become Germany's largest university by student enrollment, surpassing 130,000 students as of 2025.

IU is known for its dual studium and distance-learning programs, offering in-person study at more than 24 campuses across Germany while also serving students who need flexible schedules through a strong digital learning infrastructure.

items.name: FOM University of Applied Sciences
items.description: One of Germany's largest private higher education institutions for students who work while studying.
history: Founded in 1993 and receiving official state recognition on September 18, 1993, FOM opened its doors in 1994. Its founding purpose was to let full-time working students pursue a university education through evening and weekend programs.

Thanks to this focus, FOM grew rapidly and today operates study centers in more than 30 cities across Germany, making it one of the country's largest private higher education institutions with over 47,000 students.

With a broad range of business and economics programs, FOM also offers flexible study options that include the dual studium model, serving students who want to combine working life with a university education.

items.name: Heidelberg University (Ruprecht-Karls-Universität)
items.description: Founded in 1386, Germany's oldest and one of its most prestigious research universities.
history: Heidelberg University was founded on October 18, 1386, when Elector Ruprecht I received the Pope's permission to establish it. It is Germany's oldest university and the third to be founded in the Holy Roman Empire. Modeled after the University of Paris, it initially comprised four faculties — philosophy, theology, law, and medicine — with the Dutch scholar Marsilius of Inghen, who came from Paris, serving as its first rector.

Also known as "Ruperto Carola," the university has been home to leading scientists throughout its history, including Robert Bunsen, Hermann von Helmholtz, Gustav Kirchhoff, and Max Weber; to date, its professors have been awarded 11 Nobel Prizes.

Set in the historic city center in the shadow of Heidelberg Castle, the university is today regarded as one of Europe's strongest research universities, offering bachelor's, master's, and doctoral programs across 12 faculties and around 100 disciplines.

11 Nobel Prizes awarded to its professors to date

items.name: University of Tübingen
items.description: Founded in 1477, a classic German university-town institution strong in medicine and the natural sciences.
history: The University of Tübingen was founded in 1477 by Count Eberhard VI, following a 1476 bull from Pope Sixtus IV. It initially comprised four faculties — theology, law, medicine, and philosophy — and fourteen professorships in total. Philipp Melanchthon, one of the leading figures of the Reformation, played an important role in shaping the university's academic direction.

Over the centuries, Tübingen has counted astronomer Johannes Kepler, poet Friedrich Hölderlin, and philosophers Friedrich Schelling and G.W.F. Hegel among its students. Pope Benedict XVI also briefly studied theology there in his youth.

Located in the heart of a historic town on the Neckar River, the university today carries a strong academic tradition in medicine, natural sciences, and the humanities, having produced numerous Nobel laureates, particularly in medicine and chemistry.

Alma mater of historic figures like Kepler, Hölderlin, and Hegel

items.name: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT)
items.description: A research-driven technology university carrying the legacy of Germany's first technical higher-education institution.
history: KIT's roots trace back to the Fridericiana, founded in 1825 as Germany's first "Technische Hochschule" — the Universität Karlsruhe. It was here that Heinrich Hertz first experimentally demonstrated electromagnetic waves, and automobile pioneer Carl Benz studied at this historic institution.

In 2009, an act passed by the Baden-Württemberg state parliament merged the Universität Karlsruhe with Forschungszentrum Karlsruhe, a large-scale research institution founded in 1956, forming today's Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT).

Through this merger, KIT carries out both the teaching and research duties of a state university and the mission of a large-scale research institution within the Helmholtz Association, making it one of Germany's most comprehensive centers for technology and engineering research.

items.name: University of Freiburg
items.description: Founded in 1457, a Habsburg-legacy university strong in philosophy and the social sciences.
history: The University of Freiburg was established by a charter issued by Albert VI of the House of Habsburg on September 21, 1457, making it the second university founded in Habsburg territory after the University of Vienna. From its founding, the university taught theology, law, and medicine, along with the "Artes Liberales" (liberal arts), which formed the basis of today's faculty of humanities.

Originally named the "Albertina," the university's continued existence was secured in 1818 by a significant gift from Grand Duke Ludwig of Baden, on which occasion it was renamed the Albert-Ludwigs-Universität, its name today. As Germany's fifth-oldest university, Freiburg built a strong tradition in philosophy, philology, historical research, economics, and law.

Associated with figures such as Martin Heidegger, Edmund Husserl, Max Weber, Walter Eucken, and Nobel laureate Friedrich Hayek, Freiburg continues to carry this deep-rooted academic identity in those disciplines today.

items.name: University of Göttingen
items.description: Associated with 45 Nobel laureates, a research university at the heart of the "city of science," Göttingen.
history: Founded in 1734 by George II, King of Great Britain and Elector of Hanover, the university began lectures that same year, with its official inauguration following in 1737. Established in keeping with Enlightenment ideals, it became one of the pioneering institutions to free scientific research from church censorship.

In the 19th century, the university counted mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss and the Brothers Grimm among its faculty. In 1837, seven professors — including the Brothers Grimm — were removed from their posts after protesting the King of Hanover's expansion of his powers; the episode became known in history as the "Göttingen Seven" (Göttinger Sieben).

Göttingen is associated with 45 Nobel laureates, from quantum mechanics pioneer Max Born to mathematician Emmy Noether, 14 of whom were honored for work carried out at Göttingen itself. The oldest university in the state of Lower Saxony, Göttingen today sits at the heart of a city that carries the nickname "City of Science," with around 26,000 students.

items.name: University of Bonn
items.description: Founded in 1818, a well-established Rhineland university housed in a former electoral palace.
history: Founded on October 18, 1818, by King Frederick William III of Prussia as the Rhine University, the University of Bonn is the direct successor to the Academy of the Prince-Elector of Cologne, founded in 1777. Inspired by Wilhelm von Humboldt's principles of academic freedom and the unity of research and teaching, it quickly became one of Germany's most respected institutions.

In the 1930s, the Nazi regime forced many Jewish scholars and dissidents to leave the university; the 1944 bombing of Bonn then destroyed much of the campus. In the postwar period, the university was rebuilt and restored to its former standing.

The university's main building sits in the former Kurfürstliches Schloss (Electoral Palace), overlooking the Hofgarten park. Associated with figures such as physicist Heinrich Hertz, chemist August Kekulé, and former German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, Bonn is today one of Germany's leading universities, with around 36,000 students.

items.name: University of Cologne
items.description: Founded in 1388, one of Germany's largest traditional universities by enrollment.
history: Founded in 1388, the University of Cologne was the fourth university established in the Holy Roman Empire, after Prague (1348), Vienna (1365), and Heidelberg (1386). Its founding charter was signed by Pope Urban VI, and teaching began on January 6, 1389.

Closed during the French occupation in 1798, the university was re-established in 1919 as the "Neue Universität" (New University) — a refounding that laid the groundwork for its modern identity today.

With more than 44,000 students today, Cologne is Germany's largest traditional university by enrollment. Across six faculties and 137 degree programs, it maintains a strong academic tradition, particularly in law, economics, and the social sciences.

items.name: Technical University of Berlin
items.description: A technical university whose roots reach back to 1770, formally re-founded in 1946 to mark its present identity.
history: TU Berlin's roots trace back to the Königliche Bergakademie (Royal Mining Academy), founded in 1770, the Königliche Bauakademie (Royal Building Academy), founded in 1799, and the Königliche Gewerbeakademie (Royal Trade Academy), founded in 1821. These three institutions merged in 1879 to form the Königlich Technische Hochschule zu Berlin, with the Mining Academy incorporated in 1916.

In 1946, in a deliberate effort to document a clear break from its National Socialist past, the institution was positioned not as a reopening but as a conscious new founding, taking the name Technische Universität Berlin from that point on — the date now recognized as the university's official founding.

A member of the TU9 alliance, the university is associated with figures such as computer pioneer Konrad Zuse and chemists Carl Bosch and Fritz Haber. Located in Berlin's Charlottenburg district, TU Berlin today maintains a strong research culture in engineering and the natural sciences.

posts.title: What Are Excellence Universities and TU9? Germany's Elite Institutions
posts.excerpt: We explain 'Excellence University' (Exzellenzuniversität) and 'TU9' — two terms you'll run into often when researching universities in Germany.
body: When researching universities in Germany, you'll frequently come across terms like 'Excellence University' (Exzellenzuniversität) and 'TU9'. Both signal strong quality, but they mean different things.

'Excellence University' status is awarded under Germany's joint federal-state 'Excellence Strategy' to universities with the strongest research performance. It comes with extra research funding and international prestige — LMU Munich, TU Munich, Heidelberg University and RWTH Aachen are among the institutions holding this status.

'TU9', on the other hand, is an alliance founded in 2006 by Germany's nine most established and strongest technical universities: RWTH Aachen, TU Berlin, TU Braunschweig, TU Darmstadt, TU Dresden, Leibniz Universität Hannover, KIT (Karlsruhe), TU Munich and Universität Stuttgart. TU9 membership signals a strong research infrastructure and close industry cooperation, especially in engineering and the natural sciences.

Holding either title doesn't automatically make a university the 'best choice' for you — city, program content, language, cost of living and your personal goals matter just as much. But knowing these two labels helps you read Germany's academic landscape faster.
At Studiva, we weigh both Excellence Universities and TU9 members alongside lesser-known but strong institutions, based on your academic profile.

posts.title: What Is Dual Studium? Germany's Model for Studying While You Work
posts.excerpt: Can you earn a salary while studying? We explain Dual Studium, a higher-education model unique to Germany.
body: 'Dual Studium' is a higher-education model unique to Germany: students study at a higher-education institution while simultaneously working — and earning a salary — at a company. Theory and practice typically alternate in blocks of a few months each.

The most common provider of this model is DHBW (Duale Hochschule Baden-Württemberg); students first sign a contract with a company, then enroll at the university under that company's sponsorship. Several other universities and Hochschulen offer similar dual programs in engineering, business and IT.

The biggest advantage of Dual Studium is a regular salary throughout your studies and real work experience before graduation — tuition fees are usually waived entirely. The rate of being hired by the same company after graduation is quite high.

The trade-off is a demanding, tightly scheduled program, and you typically need to secure a company placement before enrolling — which can make the application process longer and more competitive than a standard university application.

If you want to study while earning an income, with a head start toward a guaranteed job after graduation, Dual Studium is well worth considering. At Studiva, we also help match you with a company and program that fit your profile.

posts.title: Germany Student Visa: A Step-by-Step Application Guide
posts.excerpt: We walk through the documents and steps required for a German student visa application.
body: Once you've been admitted to a German university, the most critical next step is your student visa application. The process starts with booking an appointment at the German embassy or consulate — wait times can range from weeks to months depending on the city and season, so applying early is essential.

Core documents typically include a valid passport, your university admission letter, an APS certificate (for university graduates), proof of language proficiency (German or English, depending on the program), health insurance, and proof of financial resources.

Financial resources are usually demonstrated through a blocked account (Sperrkonto): a set amount is deposited and locked, allowing the student to withdraw a fixed monthly sum over the course of a year. The required amount is updated annually — our advisors can confirm the current figure for your application period.

The visa interview usually covers your study plan, why you chose Germany and this particular program, and your financial situation; being prepared and consistent in your answers speeds up the process.

After entering Germany with your visa, you'll need to register and apply for a residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) at the local immigration office (Ausländerbehörde) within a set period. At Studiva, we support you through every step of this process, from scheduling appointments to checking your documents.

posts.title: What Is the APS Certificate and How Do You Get One?
posts.excerpt: We explain the APS process required for students to apply to a German university.
body: The APS (Akademische Prüfstelle / Examination Board) certificate is a mandatory verification process for students who completed their bachelor's or master's studies in certain countries, including Turkey, before applying to a German university. Its purpose is to confirm the authenticity of your diploma and academic record.

The process begins with uploading required documents (diploma, transcripts, high school diploma, ID, etc.) online; the documents are then reviewed, usually followed by an online or in-person interview.

Once approved, you receive an APS certificate — a mandatory part of both your university application and your student visa process; most German universities won't evaluate your application without it.
The process can take anywhere from a few weeks to a few months, so if you're planning to study in Germany, it's important to start your APS application as early as possible.
At Studiva, we manage the entire process with you, from preparing the required documents for APS to tracking your application.

posts.title: Cost of Living in Germany and the Blocked Account (Sperrkonto)
posts.excerpt: How should you plan your monthly budget in Germany, and what exactly is a blocked account (Sperrkonto)?
body: As a student in Germany, your monthly budget varies significantly by city; cities like Munich, Frankfurt or Stuttgart are notably more expensive than cities like Dresden, Braunschweig or Furtwangen.

As a general rule, a monthly budget covering accommodation, food, transport, insurance and other expenses tends to be lower in mid-sized cities and higher in major metropolitan areas; finding student housing also has a significant impact on your budget.

The 'blocked account' (Sperrkonto), a mandatory part of the student visa application, is a special bank account used to prove you can cover your basic living expenses in Germany; a set amount is deposited and locked, and the student can withdraw a fixed monthly sum from it.

Besides a blocked account, some students demonstrate financial resources through a formal declaration of commitment ('Verpflichtungserklärung') from a German resident, or a scholarship confirmation letter; which method suits you depends on your situation.
At Studiva, we build a realistic budget plan for your target city and manage the process with you — from opening a blocked account to tracking the current required amounts.

posts.title: DAAD Scholarships and Other Funding Options in Germany
posts.excerpt: Is it possible to get a scholarship to study in Germany? We round up DAAD and other funding options.
body: Studying in Germany is already more affordable than in many European countries — public universities generally charge no tuition fees — and a range of scholarship options are also available.

DAAD (Deutscher Akademischer Austauschdienst / German Academic Exchange Service) is Germany's largest and most recognized scholarship organization, offering numerous programs for students from various countries, particularly at master's and PhD level.

Beyond DAAD, options worth exploring include universities' own scholarship programs, scholarships from political foundations such as the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung or Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung, and Europe-wide exchange/funding programs like Erasmus+.

Scholarship applications typically require academic achievement, a motivation letter, reference letters, and sometimes proof of language proficiency; application deadlines are often independent of — and earlier than — university application deadlines, so it pays to start researching early.
At Studiva, we research scholarship programs that match your academic profile and help you prepare your application materials.
